scenes.name: hook
scenes.text: What if an elevator's cable snapped? In movies it falls. In real life, it's designed not to. Here's why.

scenes.name: ropes
scenes.text: Most elevators hang from several steel ropes, not one. Each rope alone is strong enough to hold the car.

scenes.name: governor
scenes.text: A separate loop of rope runs over a wheel called the speed governor, moving with the car all the time.

scenes.name: trip
scenes.text: If the car goes too fast, spinning weights in the governor fling outward, and trip a catch that grabs that rope.

scenes.name: safety
scenes.text: The grabbed rope pulls a lever on the car, which jams steel wedges against the guide rails. The car stops.

scenes.name: buffer
scenes.text: At the very bottom of the shaft, springs or oil buffers are there to soften any landing.

scenes.name: history
scenes.text: This idea goes back to Elisha Otis, who showed his safety brake in 1853, by cutting the rope while standing on the platform.

scenes.name: outro
scenes.text: Ropes, governor, wedges, buffers. Built to never fall. Follow for more on how things really work.
